> **What this case shows** — the ecosystem builds an **inter-muscle coordination
> network** from real GRABMyo forearm EMG whose edges and topology **reproduce**
> when the recording is split in half. **What reproduces, and what doesn't** —
> the coherence network reproduces near-perfectly in both its edges and its
> topology (**edge r = 0.994**, **node-strength r = 0.997**), and the wPLI and
> directed-Granger edges reproduce too; what does **not** reproduce well is the
> **partial-coherence node strength** (**0.572**) — because the partial-coherence
> graph is sparse, so each node's strength rests on a handful of edges and small
> differences between halves swing the totals. **How to read it** — in the
> figure, the paired bars are the split-half correlation of edge weights and of
> node strengths for each estimator; a bar near 1 means that half of the data
> rebuilds the same network.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — answer *"is this inter-muscle coordination structure real, or
split-specific noise?"* in three moves: **envelope** the multi-muscle EMG →
**build** the connectivity network with each estimator → **correlate** edges and
node strengths between two independent halves.
**Way of thinking** — a connectivity network is trustworthy only if *both* its
edges and its topology are stable; different estimators (coherence, partial
coherence, wPLI, directed GC) trade sensitivity for specificity differently, so
build several and trust what reproduces — and remember a **sparse** graph's node
strengths are more fragile than its edges.
**Ecosystem usage** — chain one function per role, I/O → preprocessing →
analysis (`readWFDB` → `emgEnvelope` → `emg*Network` → `emgCoordinationStructure`),
letting the shared `PhysioExperiment` data model connect them. The final section
turns this into a step-by-step you can adapt to your own recordings.
:::

## Proposition

On real GRABMyo forearm EMG, the ecosystem's inter-muscle coordination network is
reproducible across independent data halves: coherence connectivity replicates
near-perfectly (**edge r = 0.994**, **node-strength r = 0.997**), with weighted
phase-lag index (edge r = 0.835) and directed Granger causality (edge r = 0.939)
also reproducible.

## Question & goal

**The question comes from the dataset's own design.** GRABMyo records many
forearm and wrist muscles together while the hand forms gestures, built for
hand-gesture recognition and biometrics (Pradhan, He, Jiang, 2022). Recording
many muscles at once poses its own question: **which muscles co-activate — what
is the coordination *structure* behind the gestures?** A functional-connectivity
network answers that by wiring muscles that move together into a graph. But such
networks are easy to compute and easy to over-interpret, so we ask the honest
version of the question: does the ecosystem's coordination network describe
**stable** structure — does it reproduce when the recording is split in half?

## Challenge & approach

A connectivity network is only trustworthy if both its edges and its topology are
stable, and different estimators (coherence, partial coherence, wPLI, directed
Granger causality) trade sensitivity for specificity differently. The recipe
builds the 10-muscle network with each estimator, then correlates edge weights
and node strengths between two independent halves of the recording:

```
readWFDB  →  emgEnvelope  →  {coherence, partial, wPLI, directed-GC} network  →  correlate edges + nodes across halves
```

Each estimator asks a different question of the same signal — marginal
co-activation (coherence), co-activation with shared drive removed (partial
coherence), non-zero-lag phase coupling (wPLI), directional influence (GC) — so
reporting several is the point, not hedging.

## Data

**GRABMyo v1.1.0** (PhysioNet) — public
(<https://physionet.org/content/grabmyo/1.1.0/>); forearm EMG, 10-muscle
coordination network. *Pradhan A, He J, Jiang N. Multi-day dataset of forearm and
wrist electromyogram for hand gesture recognition and biometrics. Sci Data.
2022;9:733.*

## Results

![Split-half reproducibility of the muscle-coordination network for each estimator: paired bars give the correlation of edge weights and of node strengths between two independent halves of the GRABMyo recording. Directed GC has no node-strength bar; the orange label flags the weak partial-coherence node strength.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* each bar is a correlation between the two halves of the
recording — near 1 means that half rebuilds the same network. Edge-weight r asks
whether the *connections* reproduce; node-strength r asks whether the *topology*
(who is a hub) reproduces.

Split-half reproducibility of edge weights
([`artifacts/validation_split_half.csv`](artifacts/validation_split_half.csv)) and
node strengths
([`artifacts/validation_topology_split_half.csv`](artifacts/validation_topology_split_half.csv)):

| Estimator | Edge-weight r | Node-strength r |
|---|---|---|
| coherence | **0.994** | **0.997** |
| partial coherence | 0.975 | 0.572 |
| wPLI | 0.835 | 0.929 |
| directed Granger causality | 0.939 | — |

The coherence network reproduces almost perfectly in both edges and topology;
wPLI and directed-GC edges are reproducible too.

## Conclusion

On real GRABMyo EMG the ecosystem recovers a stable inter-muscle coordination
network — reproducible across independent data halves — establishing that the
connectivity structure is signal, not split-specific noise. The transferable
lesson: split the data and correlate both edges and topology before you believe a
connectivity network.

## Open questions

Partial-coherence node-strength reproducibility (0.572) trails its edge-weight
reproducibility (0.975) because the partial-coherence graph is sparse and its
node strengths are more split-sensitive. A documented method-sensitivity, not
escalated.

## Using this in your own analysis

This case is a worked example of a **connectivity-reproducibility test** — the
pattern for any "is this network real, or an artefact of one data split?"
question.

**The general recipe** (three steps, the same for any connectivity network):

1. **Envelope** each channel so the network sees co-activation over time.
2. **Build** the network with one or more estimators — coherence for marginal
   co-activation, partial coherence to remove shared drive, wPLI to discount
   zero-lag coupling, directed GC for directionality.
3. **Test stability** by rebuilding the network on two independent halves and
   correlating both the edge weights and the node strengths; trust the estimators
   whose *edges and topology* both reproduce.

**Which functions, and how they compose.** Each step is one ecosystem function,
picked by *role* — I/O → preprocessing → analysis:

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| load the forearm EMG recording | `readWFDB()` | PhysioIO |
| rectify + smooth to activation envelopes | `emgEnvelope()` | PhysioEMG |
| coherence connectivity network | `emgCoherenceNetwork()` | PhysioEMG |
| partial-coherence network | `emgPartialCoherenceNetwork()` | PhysioEMG |
| weighted phase-lag-index network | `emgWPLINetwork()` | PhysioEMG |
| directed Granger-causality network | `emgDirectedGCNetwork()` | PhysioEMG |
| topology summary (density, modules, node strength) | `emgCoordinationStructure()` | PhysioEMG |

They chain because each returns (or consumes) a `PhysioExperiment` — the shared
data model is what lets the tools snap together, so you compose an analysis by
naming the steps, not by reshaping matrices between them.

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **`freq_band`** — `c(20, 250)` is the informative surface-EMG band; content
  below ~20 Hz is movement artifact and much above is noise at this sampling rate.
- **`nperseg`, `noverlap`** — the spectral window sets the frequency resolution
  and the number of independent segments the estimate averages over; 512 samples
  at 2048 Hz is ~250 ms per window, `noverlap = 256` steps them by half.
- **Estimator choice** — coherence is sensitive but confounded by common drive;
  **partial** coherence removes shared influence (sparser graph, but its node
  strengths become split-sensitive, exactly the 0.572 above); **wPLI** discounts
  zero-lag / volume-conduction coupling; **directed GC** adds direction. Report
  several rather than betting on one.
- **Split location** — halve the recording over time and process both halves with
  the *identical* recipe, so a method difference can't masquerade as instability.

**Applying it to your own hypothesis.** Swap the GRABMyo record for your own
multi-muscle (or multi-channel) recording, keep the envelope → network →
split-half recipe, and report only the estimators whose edges *and* topology
reproduce. The same coordination question appears as a low-dimensional synergy
decomposition on this data ([`emg-synergy-grabmyo`](../emg-synergy-grabmyo/)) and
at the individual motor-unit level ([`hdemg-mu-openhdemg`](../hdemg-mu-openhdemg/)).

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioIO); library(PhysioEMG)

pe  <- readWFDB("session1_participant1_...")            # GRABMyo forearm EMG (10-muscle set)
env <- emgEnvelope(pe, method = "rms", window_ms = 50)   # rectify + smooth

# build the inter-muscle network with each estimator (coherence shown)
net   <- emgCoherenceNetwork(env, freq_band = c(20, 250), nperseg = 512L, noverlap = 256L)
coord <- emgCoordinationStructure(net$network)           # density, modules, node strengths

# split-half reproducibility: same network on each half, correlate edges + node strengths
sig  <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(env, "envelope"); half <- nrow(sig) %/% 2
n1 <- emgCoherenceNetwork(env[seq_len(half), ],        freq_band = c(20, 250))$network
n2 <- emgCoherenceNetwork(env[(half + 1):nrow(sig), ], freq_band = c(20, 250))$network
cor(n1[upper.tri(n1)], n2[upper.tri(n2)])                # edge-weight r (coherence): 0.994
cor(rowSums(n1), rowSums(n2))                            # node-strength r: 0.997
```

**Auditing the numbers.** For readers who want to verify rather than trust: every
edge-weight and node-strength split-half correlation lives in
[`artifacts/`](artifacts/), and `audit.py` re-checks each number on this page
against those files.
